entries.title: Mandarin at a glance
body: Mandarin Chinese has almost no inflection: verbs don't change for person or tense, and nouns don't change for number. Meaning comes from word order, small particles and context.
It is tonal: the pitch contour of a syllable is part of the word. The basic order is subject, verb, object, with time and place before the verb.
Pinyin is the official romanization, used for teaching and for typing characters.

examples.e: I drink tea. / I drank tea.
They drink tea. (the verb stays the same)

entries.title: The four tones
entries.body: Each syllable has one of four tones, or a light neutral tone. The same syllable with a different tone is a different word.

head: Tone
Contour
Example
rows: rising, as in a question: what?
sharply falling, as in a command

entries.title: Tone changes
entries.body: A few tones change in context. Pinyin is usually written with the original tone, so learn the rule rather than the spelling.

head: Rule
Example
rows: 你好 nǐ hǎo is said ní hǎo
不 bù → bú before a 4th tone
不是 bú shì · is not
一 yī → yí before a 4th tone
一个 yí ge · one (of something)
一天 yì tiān · one day

entries.title: Pinyin letters that fool English speakers

head: Pinyin
Sounds like
Example
rows: j, ch, sh with the tongue curled back
中 zhōng · 吃 chī · 是 shì
between English r and the s in measure
ü (u after j q x y)
去 qù · go; 绿 lǜ · green
-i after z c s zh ch sh r
a buzzing continuation of the consonant, not ee

entries.title: Simplified and Traditional characters
entries.body: Mainland China and Singapore use {Simplified} characters, introduced in the 1950s and 60s. Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau use {Traditional} characters. About a third of common characters differ; many, like 人 and 大, are the same in both.

entries.title: Radicals
entries.body: Most characters combine a meaning part (the radical) and a sound hint. Spotting the radical gives you a clue to meaning and is how paper dictionaries are ordered.

head: Radical
Meaning
Examples
rows: 河 river · 海 sea · 洗 wash
林 grove · 森 forest · 桌 table
吃 eat · 喝 drink · 叫 call
你 you · 他 he · 休 rest
说 speak · 话 words · 语 language
妈 mother · 姐 elder sister · 好 good

entries.title: Word order: time and place first
entries.body: The order is subject, time, place, verb, object. Time words can also go before the subject. Unlike English, when and where never come at the end.

examples.e: I will study at home tomorrow.

examples.r: Zuótiān wǒ zài shāngdiàn mǎi le yì běn shū.
examples.e: Yesterday I bought a book at the shop.

entries.title: Measure words
entries.body: A number or 这 / 那 (this / that) can't go straight before a noun; a measure word goes between. 个 gè is the general one. Use 两 liǎng, not 二 èr, for two of something.

head: Measure
Used for
Example
rows: 两张纸 · two sheets of paper
一杯茶 · a cup of tea

entries.title: 了, 过 and 在
entries.body: Chinese marks aspect, not tense. 了 le shows that an action is completed or a situation has changed. 过 guo means have ever done. 在 zài before a verb means in the middle of doing.

entries.title: 不 and 没
entries.body: {不} bù negates the present, the future, habits and adjectives. {没} méi negates the past and is the only way to negate 有 (have).

examples.e: I'm not going. / I won't go.

entries.title: Questions
entries.body: Add 吗 ma to a statement, or repeat the verb with 不 in between (A-not-A). Question words stay where the answer would go; there is no moving them to the front.

examples.e: Are you a student or not?

entries.title: The linking particle 的
entries.body: 的 de joins a describing word or phrase to the noun after it. It marks possession, and it turns whole clauses into descriptions; the description always comes before the noun.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: 一 yī, 二 èr, 三 sān, 四 sì, 五 wǔ, 六 liù, 七 qī, 八 bā, 九 jiǔ, 十 shí. Larger numbers are perfectly regular: 十一 is 11, 二十 is 20, 九十九 is 99. Big numbers group by ten thousands (万 wàn), not thousands.

entries.title: Characters shared with Japanese and Korean
entries.body: Japanese kanji and Korean hanja came from Chinese characters, so many words can be read across all three with different pronunciations. Japan simplified some characters its own way after 1946, so a kanji may match the Simplified form (学), the Traditional one (東), or neither (売, Simplified 卖, Traditional 賣). Hanja are Traditional.
